origins.section: The JMM Says Which Writes a Read May Return, and a Test Shows Only Some of Them
A Program Without Data Races Runs as Some Interleaving of Its Threads
A Plain long or double May Be Read Half Old, Half New
A Race Is Benign Only When Every Thread Writes the Same Value, in One Indivisible Write, Read Once

gates.says: all 4 of this quiz's answerable readings held and each was taken over the question as it stands

recorded.prompt:q-header-load-test: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-header-load-test: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-header-load-test: Page decides c: "The JLS allows 0 all the same. It treats the default 0 as a write that happens-before every action of every thread. A's store is ordered with neither of B's reads, so it doesn't count as a write between the 0 and read 2, and read 2 may return either." and "A run shows what one JIT did on one CPU; the JMM defines the outcomes your code must be correct for." The page argues with an int default 0, the quiz with a reference default null; the transfer is direct (both are default values), but the page never says 'null' itself.
recorded.prompt:q-last-seat: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-last-seat: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-last-seat: Page decides a through the rate-limiter example (every access volatile, so no data race, but a limit is still lost): "Every access to the field is volatile ... so there is no data race"; "Nothing surprising happened to memory: this is an ordinary interleaving. A checks, B checks, each creates a map and stores it"; "Sequential consistency settles which write each read sees; it doesn't make a check and the write that depends on it one step."
recorded.prompt:q-session-expiry: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-session-expiry: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-session-expiry: Page decides c: JLS 17.7: "a single write to a non-volatile long or double value is treated as two separate writes: one to each 32-bit half"; Summary: "64-bit HotSpot never tore one in three billion reads; the JLS still allows it"; Reference table: plain long/double "not guaranteed: may be split into two 32-bit halves (17.7)".
recorded.prompt:q-route-caches: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-route-caches: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-route-caches: Page decides a: "The int checksum is safe if its getter reads the field once, like String." with the conditions "Every thread writes the same value", "One write, of a type that can't tear. hash is an int", "The field is read once"; the stem supplies the read-once getter.

recorded.prompt:q-header-load-test:a: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-header-load-test:a: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-header-load-test:a: Refuted: "A run shows what one JIT did on one CPU; the JMM defines the outcomes your code must be correct for." and "No call returned 0 in three billion: allowed by the JLS, not observed here."
recorded.prompt:q-header-load-test:b: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-header-load-test:b: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-header-load-test:b: Refuted: the JLS "names no caches, registers or main memory", and "Within one thread nobody can tell, so a compiler may load the value it returns before the one it tests." The page doesn't discuss x86 read ordering, but the compiler-reordering point is enough to refute it.
recorded.prompt:q-header-load-test:d: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-header-load-test:d: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-header-load-test:d: Refuted: "Reads and writes of volatile long and double are always atomic, and so are reads and writes of references." Reference table: plain reference is atomic, "yes".
recorded.prompt:q-last-seat:b: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-last-seat:b: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-last-seat:b: Refuted: sequentially consistent means "every read seeing the latest write before it"; Reference table: a volatile "write happens-before every later read of that field"; "Sequential consistency settles which write each read sees".
recorded.prompt:q-last-seat:c: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-last-seat:c: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-last-seat:c: Refuted: sequential consistency is "as if the threads' actions ran one at a time" (actions, not method calls), and "it doesn't make a check and the write that depends on it one step. That is atomicity". Summary: "That removes reordering surprises, not check-then-act failures".
recorded.prompt:q-last-seat:d: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-last-seat:d: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-last-seat:d: Refuted by the same example: a volatile read of `limits` followed by a volatile write of `limits` lost an update; "it doesn't make a check and the write that depends on it one step". The page never says in so many words 'a volatile read plus a volatile write is not atomic', but the worked example has exactly that shape.
recorded.prompt:q-session-expiry:a: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-session-expiry:a: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-session-expiry:a: Refuted: "64-bit HotSpot never tore one in three billion reads; the JLS still allows it" and "no read was torn, so tearing is allowed by the JLS, not observed here." Minor risk: "The JLS lets a JVM split the write so that hardware without an atomic 64-bit access needs no lock" gives a hardware rationale that a reader could misread as a hardware condition; the page never says outright that the permission holds on 64-bit hardware too.
recorded.prompt:q-session-expiry:b: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-session-expiry:b: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-session-expiry:b: Refuted: "A reader can combine the high half of one write with the low half of another", and the test uses a single writer ("A writer stores values ... into a static long, and a reader counts values whose halves differ"); the byte-counter example is also one writer's successive values.
recorded.prompt:q-session-expiry:d: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-session-expiry:d: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-session-expiry:d: Refuted: "Reads and writes of volatile long and double are always atomic, and so are reads and writes of references"; Reference table: plain int, short, byte, char, boolean, float, reference are atomic, "yes"; and 17.6: "two threads writing neighbouring fields ... never overwrite each other's values".
recorded.prompt:q-route-caches:b: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-route-caches:b: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-route-caches:b: Refuted: "The long total can tear on a JVM that splits it." Summary: "a lazy long or a lazy mutable map doesn't" qualify.
recorded.prompt:q-route-caches:c: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-route-caches:c: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-route-caches:c: Refuted by analogy: "HashMap's fields aren't final, so nothing orders them before the plain reference write, and a reader may see the reference and an empty table". The page argues about HashMap, not ArrayList; the learner has to carry the 'fields aren't final' point over. Also the page's fix "an unmodifiable map built first, stored once and read once, fixes it" sits right next to option c's 'filled and then stored, complete before it', so a learner who misses that the difference is final fields could pick c.
recorded.prompt:q-route-caches:d: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-route-caches:d: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-route-caches:d: Refuted: "A map that callers keep changing after it is published is worse still: the tenant's limit showed what happens to writes into a losing copy", plus the no-ordering point for non-final fields ("nothing orders them before the plain reference write").
